newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN reports widespread gunrunning to eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN reports widespread gunrunning to eastern Zaire.

text.p: Well before the latest crisis in Eastern Zaire, weapons for Hutu rebels were flowing into the region from Europe and South Africa, with organisers of the illicit arms traffic based in Kenya, says a new U.N. report.

The weapons were procured by middlemen around the world in an operation aimed at stoking the civil war in Rwanda, said the report to the Security Council, which gave an unusual insight into widespread international arms traffic.

"Reliable and highly reliable sources in Belgium, Kenya, Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania and the United Kingdom painted a coherent picture of huge, loose, overlapping webs or more or less illicit arms deals, arms flights and arms deliveries spanning the continent from South Africa as far as Europe, particularly eastern Europe," said the report, obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.
Zaire's airport in Kinsasha, the capital, appeared to serve as a "hub for weapons shipments, some of which are reloaded onto light aircraft and redirected to Kivu" province in eastern Zaire.
The report by a four-man U.N.-appointed Commission of Inquiry is the third issued on violations of an arms embargo imposed after the 1994 ethnic massacres against Tutsis in Rwanda.
After the killings that left more than 50,000 people dead, mostly minority Tutsis, a million Hutus fled to eastern Zaire, including soldiers and militia.

The crisis escalated recently when ethnic Tutsis in Zaire fought the Zairean army with the refugees caught in the crossfire. Rwanda is accused by Zaire of helping create a Zairean Tutisi militia, presumably in response to Hutu raids into Rwanda.

In its report, the commission said hundreds of thousands of funds were raised in refugee camps in Zaire and Tanzania, often through force "war taxes" that include selling relief supplies and taking money from those employed by aid agencies.

Leaders of the Rwandan former military, including army chief General Augustin Bizimungu, held regular meetings in Nairobi hotels to organise the effort and collected hundreds of thousands of dollars in fund-raising meetings. They are also suspected of using a Nairobi plant printing conterfeit U.S. dollars.
All the Rwandans under suspicion in Kenya are travelling on passports from Zaire, the commission said.
Their aim, the report said, apparently was to invade Rwanda and at minimum to identify witnesses to the genocide who might testify on war crimes before the U.N. tribunal on Rwanda.

"The commission was given a detailed description of the ways in which genocide survivors or those who might give evidence... are identified, tracked and killed, even if they are in the custody of the Rwandan goverment," the report said.
But it said requests to both the Zairean and Kenyan governments for more information or investigations were ignored.
Among other reports the commission was looking into and awaiting responses from the governments were:
-- More details on its earlier report tracing South African weapons to the Seychelles en route to Zaire with money passing through Geneva's Union Bancaire Privee.
-- 50 anti-personnel mines manufactured in southern Italy.
-- Inquiries on two Ukrainian-registered planes with 30 tons of arms landing in Egypt en route from Bulgaria to Zaire.
-- Meetings between a French national and General Bizimungu in Zaire. France denied the government was in any way involved.
-- A Nigerian-registered plane with suspected arms stopping in Madrid and Malta en route to Goma in eastern Zaire.
-- An unidentified British-based company alleged to have been involved in transporting arms to Goma.
-- Approaches to arms industries in the Czech Republic
-- Arms deliveries from Zambia across Lake Tanganyika
